title: Barriers 2025 — Part B
source: WSU Y5 Barriers 2025 MCQ, student reconstruction; stems rewritten, tested point preserved

questions.stem: A man has months of progressive dysphagia — first to solids, now to liquids — with substantial weight loss. Examination also finds reduced sensation in the feet and absent ankle jerks.
questions.lead: What is the most likely cause of the dysphagia?
questions.explanation: Progressive solids-then-liquids dysphagia with weight loss is malignancy until proven otherwise; the neuropathy is a red herring or nutritional. Achalasia is dysphagia to both from the start; bulbar palsy affects liquids first.
questions.point: Progressive dysphagia solids → liquids with weight loss is oesophageal cancer; achalasia is to solids and liquids from the outset and neurological dysphagia starts with liquids.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of severe upper gastrointestinal bleeding?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: Peptic ulcer is the commonest single cause, accounting for roughly a third of major upper GI bleeds — down from historical figures of ~50% since H. pylori eradication and PPIs. Varices bleed harder with higher mortality but are less common; Mallory–Weiss is usually self-limiting.
questions.point: Peptic ulcer disease is the commonest single cause of severe upper GI haemorrhage (roughly a third of cases); varices are less common but carry the highest mortality per bleed.

questions.stem: A young man at a party took an unknown drug. He is sweating profusely with dilated pupils, tachycardic, hypertensive, energetic and very talkative. No psychiatric history.
questions.lead: What is the mechanism of the drug he took?
questions.explanation: Sympathomimetic toxidrome — mydriasis, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, agitation — is amphetamine-type release of NA and dopamine. Opioids constrict pupils; GABA drugs sedate; NMDA antagonists (ketamine) dissociate.
questions.point: The sympathomimetic toxidrome (dilated pupils, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, agitation) is amphetamine-type noradrenaline/dopamine release; the anticholinergic look-alike has dry skin.

questions.stem: An elderly patient with acute confusion is given diazepam.
questions.lead: What is the greatest risk?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are deliriogenic in the elderly — they prolong and deepen delirium and increase falls. They are reserved for alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium.
questions.point: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in the elderly and are avoided except for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal; non-drug measures first, low-dose antipsychotic only if unsafe.

questions.stem: A woman with a history of breast cancer presents with hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia.
questions.lead: Which statement is TRUE?
options: A raised PTH would make hypercalcaemia of malignancy less likely
Increased dietary calcium is the likely cause
Post-menopausal women normally have a raised serum calcium
questions.explanation: Malignant hypercalcaemia suppresses PTH; a raised or unsuppressed PTH points to primary hyperparathyroidism instead — which also drops phosphate. Diet does not cause hypercalcaemia in normal kidneys.
questions.point: In hypercalcaemia the PTH decides: suppressed PTH = malignancy or vitamin D excess; raised/inappropriately normal PTH = primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to the combined oral contraceptive pill in a 29-year-old?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine is an interaction, not a contraindication — enzyme induction reduces efficacy, so you change method or accept reduced reliability. Migraine with aura, current breast cancer, previous VTE and uncontrolled hypertension are all absolute contraindications (WHO/UK MEC category 4). Note the trap that was removed from this list: heavy smoking is only category 4 from age 35; below 35 it is category 2 and not a contraindication.
questions.point: Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, rifampicin) reduce COCP efficacy but are not contraindications; migraine with aura, current breast cancer, prior VTE and uncontrolled hypertension are. Smoking is only a category 4 contraindication from age 35.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old tells her GP she intends to have sex with her 15-year-old boyfriend and asks for contraception.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: You are obliged to prescribe to prevent pregnancy
Prescribe if you assess her as a mature minor
Refuse — she is under the age of consent
questions.explanation: Under Gillick/mature-minor principles a minor who understands the treatment can consent to it, and confidentiality is preserved unless there is a safety concern. Prescribing is discretionary on that assessment, not mandatory.
questions.point: A minor who demonstrates understanding (Gillick competence / mature minor) can consent to contraception confidentially; assess competence and safety rather than informing parents or refusing.

questions.stem: A woman on carbimazole for hyperthyroidism presents with fever and painful oral and buccal ulcers. Neutrophils are 0.2 ×10⁹/L.
questions.lead: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Carbimazole agranulocytosis — sore throat or mouth ulcers on an antithyroid drug means stop it and check the FBC urgently. Rare (~0.3%) but the classic exam pairing.
questions.point: Sore throat or mouth ulcers on carbimazole/propylthiouracil = suspect agranulocytosis: stop the drug and check an urgent FBC.

questions.stem: The day after thyroidectomy a patient develops cramps in the hands and perioral tingling.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Perioral paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm after thyroidectomy is hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury. Confirm and replace calcium; stridor from haematoma is the indication to open the wound, not tetany.
questions.point: Perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm after thyroidectomy = hypocalcaemia from parathyroid damage — check calcium and replace; opening the wound is for haematoma with stridor.

questions.stem: A patient with known panhypopituitarism after pituitary surgery is on once-daily thyroxine. Bloods show TSH low, free T4 low, free T3 normal.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Split the same dose into morning and evening
No change — TSH is suppressed so she is adequately replaced
questions.explanation: In secondary hypothyroidism TSH is uninterpretable — the pituitary cannot make it. Titrate to free T4 in the upper half of the range, so a low T4 means under-replacement regardless of the low TSH. One safety rule: glucocorticoid replacement must be adequate before thyroxine is increased, because thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate an adrenal crisis.
questions.point: In secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism TSH is useless — dose thyroxine to free T4 in the upper half of normal; always ensure glucocorticoid replacement is adequate first, or raising thyroxine can precipitate adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A patient has a smooth, diffusely enlarged goitre. TSH is mildly elevated with a normal free T4.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diffuse smooth goitre with subclinical hypothyroidism is Hashimoto's — confirm with anti-TPO. Graves would suppress TSH; multinodular is nodular by definition.
questions.point: A smooth diffuse goitre with a raised TSH and normal T4 (subclinical hypothyroidism) is Hashimoto thyroiditis — check anti-TPO antibodies.

questions.stem: A patient has weak knee extension, weak ankle inversion, reduced sensation over the medial calf and medial malleolus, and a diminished knee jerk.
questions.lead: Which nerve root is affected?
questions.explanation: Knee jerk plus medial leg sensation is L4. L5 is dorsum of foot/great toe with foot drop and no reflex; S1 is lateral foot and the ankle jerk.
questions.point: L4 = knee jerk, quadriceps and medial leg; L5 = dorsiflexion, great toe and dorsum of foot with no reflex; S1 = ankle jerk, plantarflexion and lateral foot.

questions.stem: A woman describes hand pain and numbness that wakes her at night and is worse in the morning, easing when she shakes the hand. Tapping over the wrist crease reproduces it.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nocturnal paraesthesia relieved by shaking, with a positive Tinel's at the wrist, is median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel.
questions.point: Nocturnal hand paraesthesia relieved by shaking, positive Tinel's/Phalen's at the wrist = carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve).

questions.stem: A woman has a thin, milky vaginal discharge with a fishy odour but no itch or pain.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fishy, non-irritant discharge is BV (clue cells, pH >4.5). Candida itches with a curdy discharge; trichomonas is frothy, green and irritant.
questions.point: Fishy-smelling thin grey discharge without irritation = bacterial vaginosis (pH >4.5, clue cells); candida itches and is curdy, trichomonas is frothy and irritant.

questions.stem: Which statement about cortisol is TRUE?
questions.lead: Choose one.
options: ACTH drives both cortisol and aldosterone secretion equally
Cortisol circulates mostly bound to cortisol-binding globulin and albumin
Cortisol is stored in secretory granules
questions.explanation: ~90% of cortisol is protein-bound (CBG > albumin). It acts on intracellular receptors, peaks in the early morning, is synthesised on demand not stored, and ACTH has little effect on aldosterone — which is why secondary adrenal insufficiency spares potassium.
questions.point: Cortisol is ~90% protein-bound (CBG, albumin), acts on intracellular receptors, peaks early morning; ACTH barely affects aldosterone, so secondary AI spares potassium.

questions.stem: An older man is waking several times a night to pass urine.
questions.lead: What is the most useful initial investigation?
questions.explanation: Nocturia is first characterised with a frequency-volume chart: it separates nocturnal polyuria (large volumes — cardiac, renal, sleep apnoea) from small-volume storage symptoms of BPH. Treatment follows from that.
questions.point: For nocturia the first step is a bladder diary — nocturnal polyuria (large volumes) has medical causes and is not fixed by prostate drugs.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has never been reliably dry overnight and wets the bed most nights. He is dry by day, has no daytime urgency, and urinalysis and examination are normal. Reward charts and fluid advice have not helped.
questions.lead: What is the recommended first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: This is primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis. Once advice on fluids, toileting and reward systems has failed, the alarm is first-line treatment from about age 6–7 with the best long-term cure rate; desmopressin is for short-term cover (sleepovers, camps) or alarm failure. An alarm is not appropriate if wetting is infrequent (<1–2 nights a week).
questions.point: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis from ~6–7 years: enuresis alarm is first-line treatment after fluid/toileting/reward advice has failed; desmopressin for short-term need or alarm failure. Secondary enuresis (previously dry ≥6 months) needs a search for a trigger first.

questions.stem: A dependent 75-year-old with Alzheimer's in a nursing home has refused food for two days but takes fluids. Examination of the mouth shows white plaques on the tongue and palate that scrape off leaving a red base.
questions.lead: What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Painful oral candidiasis is a reversible cause of food refusal in the frail — treat it before escalating. NG feeding in advanced dementia does not improve outcomes.
questions.point: New food refusal in advanced dementia: look in the mouth — oral candidiasis is treated with a topical antifungal (miconazole 2% gel first-line in Australia, nystatin as the alternative) plus mouth care; NG feeding in advanced dementia does not improve survival.

questions.stem: A post-operative patient has been vomiting for two days. Bloods: Na 138, Cl 92, HCO3 34, K 3.0.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate fluid over the next 4 hours?
questions.explanation: Vomiting produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; the correction is chloride and potassium — saline with KCl. Dextrose-based fluids supply neither. Hartmann's is wrong here not for want of chloride (it has 111 mmol/L) but because its lactate is metabolised to bicarbonate, worsening the alkalosis, and it contains only 5 mmol/L of potassium.
questions.point: Vomiting causes hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — replace with 0.9% saline plus potassium; avoid Hartmann's because its lactate becomes bicarbonate and it carries only 5 mmol/L K.

questions.stem: A healthy young man with no medications or comorbidities (ASA 1) is booked for elective inguinal hernia repair, an intermediate-grade procedure.
questions.lead: Which pre-operative investigations are required?
questions.explanation: For an ASA 1 patient having intermediate surgery, no routine investigations are indicated — NICE NG45 and Choosing Wisely Australia both say tests are driven by comorbidity and procedure, not ritual. (In a woman of childbearing potential, pregnancy status must still be established.)
questions.point: Healthy ASA 1 patients having minor surgery need no routine pre-operative investigations — tests are indicated by comorbidity and procedure, not by default.
